---
title: "Architecture"
---

sasonr treats SAS as the only source language and R as the execution
engine. Nothing is translated "once and handed over": the SAS program is
parsed and executed every time, and the generated R code can be inspected.

```
SAS source
  │
  ├─ 1 Lexer (state machine)
  │      strings, comments, name/date/hex literals, special missing values,
  │      DATALINES blocks, macro tokens
  │
  ├─ 2 Macro processor (pull-based)
  │      %LET, &&-resolution, %MACRO/%MEND, %IF/%DO, quoting functions,
  │      global/local symbol tables. It yields one complete step at a time;
  │      after the step runs, CALL SYMPUT(X) and SQL INTO: values are written
  │      back before expansion continues.
  │
  ├─ 3 Parser → faithful AST
  │      recursive descent for statements, Pratt parser for expressions with
  │      the SAS operator precedence (including comparison chains, IN, ><, <>)
  │      IF/ELSE, DO/END, SELECT/WHEN are kept as written; desugaring happens
  │      in a separate lowering step.
  │
  ├─ 4 Execution
  │      DATA step → generated tidyverse code (L1 / L2 / L3, see below)
  │      PROC SQL  → own SQL parser; DuckDB for joins and grouping,
  │                  SAS semantics (missing values, remerge, CALCULATED) in R
  │      PROC SORT, PRINT, MEANS/SUMMARY, FREQ, TRANSPOSE, CONTENTS,
  │      DATASETS, APPEND, DELETE, FORMAT → R implementations
  │
  └─ 5 Runtime: SAS value semantics, formats/informats, functions,
         variable attributes, _ERROR_ and SAS-style log notes
```

## DATA step compilation levels

The goal is identical end-to-end results, not a replica of the program data
vector, so each step is compiled to the fastest form that is provably
equivalent:

| Level | Used when | Generated code |
|---|---|---|
| **L1** | no cross-row state | `dplyr::mutate()`, `filter()`, `select()` |
| **L2** | recognised patterns: BY groups with `FIRST.`/`LAST.`, `RETAIN` accumulators, baseline carry-forward, unconditional `LAG` | grouped vectorised code |
| **L3** | anything else (conditional `LAG`, `OUTPUT` to several data sets, `DO` loops creating rows, ...) | an explicit row loop that follows SAS execution rules |

The level is decided by analysing the AST. If a vectorised step meets a
condition that needs row-by-row diagnostics (for example invalid data that
sets `_ERROR_`), it is re-run as L3.

## The SAS session

Everything a SAS program can change lives in one session object
(`SasSession`, an R6 class), never in package-level variables:

| Component | Contents |
|---|---|
| WORK | data sets (tibbles), their metadata (types, lengths, formats, labels), PROC SQL views, `_LAST_` |
| Format catalog | user formats and informats from PROC FORMAT |
| Macro | global symbol table, local frames, macro definitions, automatic macro variables (`SYSCC`, `SYSERR`, `SQLOBS`, ...) |
| Options | `LINESIZE`, `NOTES`, `SYNTAXCHECK`, the SAS 9.4 release, and the fixed values sasonr implements (`YEARCUTOFF=1940`, `ERRORS=20`, `MISSING=.`, UTF-8) |
| Titles, filerefs | `TITLE` lines, `FILENAME` assignments |
| ODS | destinations and OUTPUT/SELECT/EXCLUDE requests (reserved for the clinical procedures) |
| SQL back end | the DuckDB connection, opened on first use and closed with the session |
| Sinks | the cumulative log and listing of all submissions |
| Diagnostics | compile-time NOTEs of the step being translated; run-time state of the step being run (`_ERROR_` flag, data-error NOTEs, missing-value and math-error counters, observations read, PRXPARSE ids) |

`sas_run(code)` creates a throw-away session; `sas_session()` creates one
that several `sas_run(code, session = s)` calls share, like submissions in
an interactive SAS session (each submission still starts outside
syntax-check mode). `sas_work()`, `sas_meta()`, `sas_macro_vars()`,
`sas_log()` and `sas_listing()` read a session.

The generated step code does not take the session as an argument. The engine
binds the session for the duration of a submission and restores the previous
binding on exit; the run-time helpers that generated code calls
(`sas_err_sync()`, `sas_put_line()`, the functions and formats) read the
bound session. Two sessions used alternately therefore never see each
other's state, and a `sas_run()` nested inside a running step gets its own
session without disturbing the outer one. Function-layer calls made outside
any run (`sas_f_round()` in your own code) use a separate default session.

Parsed programs, translations and results are plain S3 values; the function,
format and procedure-option registries are built once at load time and are
never changed by a run.

## Why not regular expressions

SAS syntax is not a regular language: nested `DO`/`END` blocks, nested
parentheses, operator precedence, context-dependent keywords (`set`, `if`
and `end` can be variable names) and macro expansion all require a real
lexer and parser. Regex-based translators reach a ceiling quickly and need
a fallback such as a language model; sasonr is fully deterministic instead.

## Fail loud

Every statement, option, function and procedure is either implemented and
verified against SAS output, or rejected with a `sasonr_unsupported`
condition that names the feature and the SAS line. Silent approximation is
treated as a bug.
